symptom: A directory pathname can be moved and replaced by a symlink after a publisher has opened it. A synthetic Linux child using a pre-opened O_DIRECTORY|O_NOFOLLOW directory FD for both renameat2 endpoints kept publication in the original moved directory, left the decoy target untouched, and allowed strict SDK readback. This is a bounded namespace probe, not a production writer or power-loss guarantee.
lesson: A pre-opened directory descriptor is bound to the directory object, not the mutable pathname. Relative renameat2 on the same directory FD can preserve single-link no-replace publication when the old parent pathname is moved and replaced by a symlink; a path-based lookup would have a different authority boundary. The record may nevertheless become unreachable under the original canonical path.
guardrail: For any future Linux-native candidate, pin a reviewed directory FD using O_DIRECTORY and O_NOFOLLOW and use dirfd-relative names, then independently verify expected directory identity, consumer-visible canonical reachability, and failure behavior. This fixture does not clear ancestor symlink chains, mount moves, cross-filesystem semantics, crash durability, staged-file cleanup, or native integration. Never auto-delete by stale pathname, relax strict readback, or connect to production/BUY.
